title: Judges 11:12–28
context: Before fighting, Jephthah sends messengers to the king of Ammon, who claims Israel took his land between the Arnon and the Jabbok. Jephthah answers with a history lesson drawn from Numbers 20–22. Israel went around Edom and Moab, never entered Moab’s border, and took the territory from Sihon king of the Amorites when Sihon attacked them. He argues that the LORD gave Israel the land, that Balak of Moab never contested it, and that Israel had held it for a long time. He appeals to the LORD the Judge to decide between them. The figure of three hundred years in verse 26 raises chronology questions that interpreters answer in different ways. The mention of Chemosh in verse 24 is a debater’s argument from the king’s own point of view, not an endorsement of another god. Both traditions value the passage as a model of seeking peace and appealing to justice before war, grounded in God’s gift of the land.

verses.text: Jephthah sent messengers to the king of the children of Ammon, saying, “What do you have to do with me, that you have come to me to fight against my land?”
verses.arminianNotes:
Jephthah sends messengers to the king of Ammon, asking why he has come to fight. Diplomacy comes before war.

Arminian readers note that Jephthah first seeks a peaceful resolution, giving the king a real opportunity to withdraw.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers note that the law commanded offering peace before battle in some circumstances (Deuteronomy 20:10), and Jephthah’s approach reflects that spirit.

Both traditions commend seeking peace and resolving disputes by reason and justice before resorting to force.

verses.text: The king of the children of Ammon answered the messengers of Jephthah, “Because Israel took away my land when he came up out of Egypt, from the Arnon even to the Jabbok, and to the Jordan. Now therefore restore that territory again peaceably.”
verses.arminianNotes:
The king of Ammon claims that Israel took his land from the Arnon to the Jabbok and the Jordan when coming out of Egypt, and demands its peaceful return. He presents a historical grievance.

Arminian readers note that Jephthah engages the claim seriously rather than dismissing it, showing respect for truth in disputes.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers note that historical claims can be used to justify aggression, and that truthful history matters in matters of justice. Disputes over land are rarely settled by force alone.

Both traditions see the importance of accurate memory in resolving conflict.

verses.text: Jephthah sent messengers again to the king of the children of Ammon;
verses.arminianNotes:
Jephthah sends messengers again to the king of Ammon. He persists in diplomacy.

Arminian readers note Jephthah’s patience: he does not immediately take up arms but tries again to reason with the king. Seeking peace twice is not weakness but restraint.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers note that persistent appeals for peace reflect God’s own patience with nations before judgment. Jephthah’s second message is detailed and careful.

Both traditions see persistence in seeking peace as a virtue, a principle Christians apply to resolving conflicts in every area of life (compare Romans 12:18).

verses.text: and he said to him, “Jephthah says: Israel didn’t take away the land of Moab, nor the land of the children of Ammon;
verses.arminianNotes:
Jephthah says that Israel did not take the land of Moab or Ammon. He begins his argument with a direct denial.

Arminian readers note that Jephthah grounds his case in Israel’s past obedience: Israel respected the borders of Moab and Ammon as God had commanded (Deuteronomy 2:9, 19).
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers note that God himself had set those borders and forbidden Israel to take them. Israel’s conduct followed his word.

Both traditions read the denial as an appeal to the facts of history recorded in Numbers and Deuteronomy.

verses.text: but when they came up from Egypt, and Israel went through the wilderness to the Red Sea, and came to Kadesh,
verses.arminianNotes:
When Israel came from Egypt through the wilderness to the Red Sea and to Kadesh, the journey began. Jephthah retells the story.

Arminian readers note that Jephthah’s retelling shows knowledge of Israel’s history and the importance of remembering what God has done.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers note that the history of the wilderness journey is part of Israel’s identity and testimony. Jephthah uses it to explain Israel’s claim.

Both traditions value the use of Scripture’s history to shape present decisions, a practice that runs throughout the Bible.

verses.text: then Israel sent messengers to the king of Edom, saying, ‘Please let me pass through your land;’ but the king of Edom didn’t listen. In the same way, he sent to the king of Moab, but he refused; so Israel stayed in Kadesh.
verses.arminianNotes:
Israel asked Edom and Moab for passage and were refused, so they stayed at Kadesh. Israel did not force its way.

Arminian readers note that Israel respected the refusal of Edom and Moab, choosing patience over conflict (compare Numbers 20:14–21).
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers note that Israel’s restraint reflected God’s command not to fight these nations (Deuteronomy 2:4–9). The appeal to Moab is not narrated in Numbers but is consistent with it.

Both traditions see in Israel’s restraint an example of respecting others’ rights.

verses.text: Then they went through the wilderness, and went around the land of Edom, and the land of Moab, and came by the east side of the land of Moab, and they encamped on the other side of the Arnon; but they didn’t come within the border of Moab, for the Arnon was the border of Moab.
verses.arminianNotes:
Israel went around Edom and Moab, camped beyond the Arnon, and did not enter Moab’s border. The Arnon was Moab’s boundary.

Arminian readers note the care Israel took to avoid wronging its neighbors, even at the cost of a longer journey.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers note that God’s guidance led Israel around rather than through, showing that his purposes include respect for the boundaries he set.

Both traditions read the verse as evidence that Israel’s claim to the land rested on a just history rather than on aggression against Moab or Ammon.

verses.text: Israel sent messengers to Sihon king of the Amorites, the king of Heshbon; and Israel said to him, ‘Please let us pass through your land to my place.’
verses.arminianNotes:
Israel asked Sihon king of the Amorites for passage to its place. Again, Israel sought peaceful passage.

Arminian readers note that Israel offered Sihon a real choice, as recorded in Numbers 21:21–22. Sihon was free to grant or refuse it.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers note that the land at issue was taken from Sihon, not from Ammon or Moab, which is the heart of Jephthah’s argument.

Both traditions read the verse as part of a consistent pattern: Israel sought peace and fought only when attacked.

verses.text: But Sihon didn’t trust Israel to pass through his border; but Sihon gathered all his people together, and encamped in Jahaz, and fought against Israel.
verses.arminianNotes:
Sihon refused, gathered his people at Jahaz, and fought Israel. The war began with Sihon’s choice.

Arminian readers note that Sihon’s refusal and attack were his own decisions, leading to his defeat. Responsibility for the war rests with the one who started it.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers note that Deuteronomy 2:30 says the LORD hardened Sihon’s spirit so that he would be delivered into Israel’s hand, holding divine purpose and human choice together.

Both traditions affirm Sihon’s responsibility and God’s rule over the outcome.

verses.text: The LORD, the God of Israel, delivered Sihon and all his people into the hand of Israel, and they struck them. So Israel possessed all the land of the Amorites, the inhabitants of that country.
verses.arminianNotes:
The LORD delivered Sihon and his people into Israel’s hand, and Israel possessed the land of the Amorites. The victory is credited to God.

Arminian readers note that Jephthah attributes the land to God’s gift, not Israel’s strength.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers note that the LORD, the God of Israel, is named as the one who acted. The land belongs to Israel because God gave it.

Both traditions see Jephthah’s argument grounded in God’s action in history, which is the foundation of Israel’s claim.

verses.text: They possessed all the border of the Amorites, from the Arnon even to the Jabbok, and from the wilderness even to the Jordan.
verses.arminianNotes:
Israel possessed the Amorite territory from the Arnon to the Jabbok and from the wilderness to the Jordan. The boundaries match the king’s claim.

Arminian readers note that Jephthah carefully shows that the same land the king claims was taken from Sihon, not from Ammon.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers note that the precise boundaries show Jephthah’s command of the facts. His case is built on history, not assertion. Precision serves justice better than slogans.

Both traditions value careful, truthful argument in resolving disputes.

verses.text: So now the LORD, the God of Israel, has dispossessed the Amorites from before his people Israel, and should you possess them?
verses.arminianNotes:
The LORD, the God of Israel, has dispossessed the Amorites, so should Ammon possess them? Jephthah presses the point.

Arminian readers note that Jephthah argues from God’s gift: what God has given, no one else has the right to take.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers note that Jephthah acknowledges God’s sovereignty over the land. The question is not human strength but God’s decision.

Both traditions affirm that God is the ultimate owner of the land and the one who distributes it among nations (compare Deuteronomy 32:8).

verses.text: Won’t you possess that which Chemosh your god gives you to possess? So whoever the LORD our God has dispossessed from before us, them will we possess.
verses.arminianNotes:
Jephthah asks whether the king will not possess what Chemosh his god gives him, so Israel will possess what the LORD has given. This is an argument from the king’s own perspective.

Arminian readers note that Jephthah reasons with the king on his own terms, without endorsing Chemosh as a true god.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers note that Chemosh is elsewhere named as the god of Moab (Numbers 21:29), which may reflect the disputed land’s earlier history or a broader reference.

Both traditions read the verse as rhetorical, not as a statement that other gods are real.

verses.text: Now are you anything better than Balak the son of Zippor, king of Moab? Did he ever strive against Israel, or did he ever fight against them?
verses.arminianNotes:
Jephthah asks whether the king is better than Balak son of Zippor, king of Moab, who never fought Israel over this land. He appeals to precedent.

Arminian readers note that Balak’s attempt to curse Israel failed (Numbers 22–24), and that he did not go to war over the territory.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers note that Balak’s inability to curse Israel showed God’s protection of his people. Jephthah uses this history to strengthen his case.

Both traditions read the appeal as reasonable argument grounded in the shared history of the region.

verses.text: Israel lived in Heshbon and its towns, and in Aroer and its towns, and in all the cities that are along the side of the Arnon for three hundred years! Why didn’t you recover them within that time?
verses.arminianNotes:
Israel lived in Heshbon, Aroer, and the cities along the Arnon for three hundred years, so why did Ammon not recover them then? The figure raises chronology questions.

Arminian readers note that the number may be a round figure or a rhetorical approximation, and interpreters reckon it differently.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers likewise note that the chronology of Judges is debated, and the three hundred years has been explained in various ways.

Both traditions hold the figure cautiously and focus on Jephthah’s point: the claim had long gone uncontested.

verses.text: Therefore I have not sinned against you, but you do me wrong to war against me. May the LORD the Judge be judge today between the children of Israel and the children of Ammon.”
verses.arminianNotes:
Jephthah says he has not sinned against the king, who wrongs him by making war, and he appeals to the LORD the Judge to decide. God is named as the true judge.

Arminian readers note that Jephthah submits the dispute to God’s justice, trusting God to decide fairly.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers note that this is a notable use of the title Judge for the LORD in a book about human judges. God is the ultimate ruler.

Both traditions see here the conviction that God governs the affairs of nations and judges between them.

verses.text: However, the king of the children of Ammon didn’t listen to the words of Jephthah which he sent him.
verses.arminianNotes:
The king of Ammon does not listen to Jephthah’s words. Diplomacy fails.

Arminian readers note that the king had a real opportunity to choose peace, and his refusal makes him responsible for the war.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers note that human stubbornness does not frustrate God’s purposes. The war that follows will accomplish God’s deliverance.

Both traditions read the king’s refusal as a sober reminder that efforts for peace are not always received, yet they remain right to pursue.
